title: Oracle Stock Is Now An AI Infrastructure Play: Is The Price Of Admission Too High?
excerpt: The company has a backlog of contracted revenue that dwarfs its peers, but it comes with a striking capital investment plan and near-term pressure on its pro...
content_html:
Trefis Team

Tue, August 25, 2026 at 10:49 AM PDT 4 min read

The company has a backlog of contracted revenue that dwarfs its peers, but it comes with a striking capital investment plan and near-term pressure on its profits.

Oracle (ORCL) just booked future business on a scale that is difficult to comprehend. The company's backlog of contractual commitments, what it calls Remaining Performance Obligations, now stands at $638 billion. That figure, driven by an explosion in demand for its cloud infrastructure to power artificial intelligence, provides a multi-year revenue pipeline at a scale rarely seen in enterprise tech. Following a 38% decline over the trailing twelve months, the stock currently trades about 56% below its 52-week high. The practical question for an investor today is what it means to buy into a company in the midst of such a monumental, capital-intensive pivot.

What The Market Is Charging

To buy Oracle stock today, you are paying a clear premium for that growth story. The stock trades at a price-to-sales ratio of 6.1, nearly double the S&P 500's multiple of 3.3. Its price-to-earnings ratio of 24.0 is also slightly ahead of the market's 23.2. This isn't a bargain bin valuation; it's the price the market assigns to a company it believes is at the front end of a large growth cycle. The market is paying up for the visibility provided by that large backlog and for management's guidance of 34% revenue growth in the coming fiscal year. For this premium to make sense, Oracle has to execute on its ambitious build-out and convert those contracts into profitable revenue without major delays or cost overruns.

The Business Underneath

What you get for that price is a business firing on its new growth engine. The driver is Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), where revenue grew 93% in the last quarter, fueled by what management calls "strong demand for both AI workloads and our database services." In that quarter alone, the company signed $67 billion in new AI infrastructure contracts. This is the source of that large backlog. But this growth requires an extraordinary amount of capital. Management plans a net cash outlay for capital expenditures of around $70 billion for fiscal year 2027. To help pay for it, the company expects to raise around $40 billion in new debt and equity. This is happening at a company where debt already sits at 38% of its market value, compared to 19.1% for the typical S&P 500 company. While the business generates high margins and strong operating cash flow, its growth re-acceleration heavily depends on the success and efficient execution of this investment cycle.
